topic: Exclusive upper bound in binary search

items.prompt: In a binary search written with an exclusive upper bound, what does `hi` hold when the search starts?
items.answer: a.length — one past the last index

items.prompt: Which loop condition goes with an exclusive `hi`?
Complete the loop condition so every element is still searched and nothing past the end is read.

notes.text: one past the end, not the last index

blocks.failure: With `lo <= hi` the last step reads a[a.length], which is undefined — search([4], 4) then returns -1.

items.prompt: This effect adds a listener on every render. Which line has to change?
items.answer: the closing line of the effect — it needs a dependency array

blocks.why: With no dependency array the effect re-runs after every render, adding a listener each time.
blocks.failure: After ten renders there are ten resize listeners and the first nine are unreachable.

items.prompt: Why is an exclusive upper bound easier to get right than an inclusive one?
items.rubric: Must mention: hi = length needs no -1; the loop ends when lo === hi; no element is read twice.

items.prompt: With an exclusive bound, what is true of `lo` and `hi` when the loop exits without a match?
A sliding window keeps `end` as the first index NOT yet in the window. What is the window's length?
Which change turns an exclusive-bound search into an off-by-one?
options: let hi = a.length - 1, keeping while (lo < hi)
